title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 6)
summary: NH continues his Hagakure reading on audacious self-belief, avoiding pleasure without effort, gratitude for life, love of home, owning your choices instead of imitating, being prepared to die, and never giving up. He ties each to lifting: verbalize your ambitions, know why you do each exercise, and treat training as a path with no finish line.
claims: Believe audaciously that you are the best; this is not arrogance but the only way to pursue greatness, like a perfect body
It doesn't matter whether you really are or will become the best; the belief is what carries you forward
People who feel threatened by your greatness are misguided and should be inspired by it instead; keep them out of your life
You must verbalize a goal before it manifests; a world champion said he would become champion before he did
Eating out of boredom makes you fat; pleasures that are not preceded by effort are usually toxic
People who openly complain about being alive without illness or pain baffle him; be grateful for the chance to live
He prefers societies where people love their homeland and dislikes those who despise their country while praising places they don't know
Being open to other ideas completes you, but flip-flopping to every new idea is walking in circles
His real home is a small mountain village where people work the fields and hunt; big cities are home to no one
Doing exercises or programs without knowing why, just imitating someone, is the worst approach; a mistake that comes from your own reasoning is better, because you own it
Imitators blame their guru when they get hurt, then jump to another; own your training, and if it fails go back to the drawing board
If attacked, fighting back often makes aggressors flee, because they look for prey that won't resist
Being at peace with death marks the first day of your real life, an idea shared with Stoicism
Never give up: losing is not falling but refusing to get up, so if you keep getting up you can't be beaten
Don't fixate on endpoint goals like lifting a certain weight; the path is infinite, and anyone claiming to have reached their limit is lazy or doesn't understand the body
Be an educated barbarian: devoted to study, never content, critical of everything
